{{Short description|Axiom in probability theory}}
{{Use American English|date=September 2026}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=September 2026}}
{{inline|date=May 2024}}
In [[probability theory]], '''Luce's choice axiom''' states that the relative [[odds]] of selecting one item over another from a pool of many items are not affected by the presence or absence of other items in the pool. Selection of this kind is said to have "[[independence of irrelevant alternatives|independence from irrelevant alternatives]]" (IIA).<ref name=twenty>{{Cite journal |last=Luce |first=R.Duncan |date=June 1977 |title=The choice axiom after twenty years|journal=Journal of Mathematical Psychology |language=en |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=215–233 |doi=10.1016/0022-2496(77)90032-3}}</ref> It was formulated by [[R. Duncan Luce]] in 1959.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Luce |first=R. Duncan |title=Individual choice behavior : a theoretical analysis |publisher=Dover Publications |year=2005 |isbn=0-486-44136-9 |location=Mineola, N.Y. |oclc=874031603}}</ref>

==Overview==
Consider a set <math>X</math> of possible outcomes, and consider a selection rule such that for any <math>a\in A \subset X</math> with <math>A</math> a finite set, the selector selects <math>a</math> from <math>A</math> with probability <math>P(a \mid A)</math>.

Luce proposed two choice axioms. The first one is usually called "[[Independence of irrelevant alternatives|independence from irrelevant alternatives]]" (IIA), and the second one is usually referred to as "Luce's choice axiom".<ref name=twenty/>

# '''Independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA)''':
#: For any <math>a, b \in B \subset A</math>, if <math>P(a\mid A) = 0, P(b\mid A) > 0</math>, then we still have <math>P(a\mid B) = 0</math>.
# '''Path independence''':
#: For any <math>a \in B \subset A</math>, <math display="block">P(a \mid A) = P(a\mid B)\sum_{b\in B}P(b\mid A)</math>

Note that IIA implies path independence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Luce |first=R. Duncan |date=2008-12-02 |title=Luce's choice axiom |journal=Scholarpedia |language=en |volume=3 |issue=12 |pages=8077 |doi=10.4249/scholarpedia.8077 |issn=1941-6016|doi-access=free |bibcode=2008SchpJ...3.8077L }}</ref>

===Matching law formulation===
{{see|Matching law}}
Define the [[matching law]] selection rule <math>P(a\mid A) = \frac{u(a)}{\sum_{a'\in A} u(a')}</math>, for some "value" function <math>u: A \to (0, \infty)</math>. This is sometimes called the [[Softmax function|softmax]] function, or the [[Boltzmann distribution]].

'''Theorem''': Any matching law selection rule satisfies Luce's choice axiom. Conversely, if <math>P(a\mid A)> 0</math> for all <math>a\in A \subset X</math>, then Luce's choice axiom implies that it is a matching law selection rule.

==Applications==
In [[econometrics]] and [[marketing science]], this axiom provides the theoretical foundation for models that calculate a consumer's probability of choosing one brand over another based on its [[Utility (economics)|utility]].{{sfn|Guadagni|Little|1982}}

In [[Behaviorism|behavioral psychology]], it is used to model response behavior in the form of [[matching law]].

In [[cognitive science]], it is used to model approximately rational decision processes.
